meta.titre: Predicate Logic and Symbolisation: translating A, E, I, O, only and all-but statements with quantifiers

sections.contenu_markdown: At a market in Bamenda a seller says that every yam on her stall is fresh, and a buyer replies that some of the yams on her stall are not fresh. Ordinary language hides the logic of such claims, and propositional logic with letters such as $P$ and $Q$ cannot see inside them. Predicate logic opens the statement and shows its structure with quantifiers. A Level Paper 1 and Paper 3 regularly ask you to translate English statements into this notation using given letters, and every mark depends on choosing the right connective. This course gives you the translation rules and the checks.

items: The symbols of propositional logic are $\sim$ (not), $\cdot$ (and), $\vee$ (or), $\supset$ (if... then) and $\equiv$ (equivalent to).
A predicate is a property or relation that can be said of an individual, such as being human or being a teacher.
The four standard categorical forms are A (all), E (no), I (some) and O (some are not).

sections.titre: Propositional functions, quantifiers and the translation rules
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Propositional functions and quantifiers
A propositional function such as $Tx$ ("$x$ is a trader") is neither true nor false. It becomes a proposition in two ways. By substitution of a constant: $Ta$ says that a particular individual $a$ is a trader. By quantification: the universal quantifier $(x)$ (also written $\forall x$) means for every $x$, and the existential quantifier $(\exists x)$ means that there is at least one $x$.

### The four standard forms
| English | Symbolic form |
|---|---|
| All $S$ are $P$ | $(x)(Sx \supset Px)$ |
| No $S$ are $P$ | $(x)(Sx \supset \sim Px)$ |
| Some $S$ are $P$ | $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot Px)$ |
| Some $S$ are not $P$ | $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot \sim Px)$ |

The key rule: the universal quantifier goes with the conditional $\supset$, and the existential quantifier goes with the conjunction $\cdot$. Words such as every, each, any and all signal a universal statement, and some, certain, at least one and there is signal an existential one.

### Quantifier exchange
$\sim(x)Fx \equiv (\exists x)\sim Fx$ and $\sim(\exists x)Fx \equiv (x)\sim Fx$. Therefore "No $S$ are $P$" can also be written $\sim(\exists x)(Sx \cdot Px)$, "All $S$ are $P$" can be written $\sim(\exists x)(Sx \cdot \sim Px)$, and "Not all $S$ are $P$" is $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot \sim Px)$.

### Special expressions
- "Only $S$ are $P$" and "None but $S$ are $P$": $(x)(Px \supset Sx)$. The terms are reversed.
- "All but $S$ are $P$" and "All except $S$ are $P$": at least $(x)(\sim Sx \supset Px)$; the fuller reading adds that no $S$ are $P$, that is, $(x)(Sx \supset \sim Px)$.
- Words such as "few" are not standard; follow the convention you were taught, and state it in your answer.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question supplies letters, for example Dx for x is a dog and Ax for x is an animal.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Keep the letters exactly as supplied and use the same variable $x$ throughout. Identify the quantifier word, then the subject class and the predicate class, then choose $\supset$ for a universal and $\cdot$ for an existential. Read your formula back in words to check it. Do not forget the quantifier: $Sx \supset Px$ alone is an open function, not a proposition.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the statement names individuals, or joins statements with and, or, if.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A singular statement uses a constant and needs no quantifier: "Abraham is a father" is $Fa$. A compound statement joins singular statements with the usual connectives: "Abraham is a father and Frida is a mother" is $Fa \cdot Mf$. When the statement mixes both kinds, translate each part and join the parts.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must show that two translations are equivalent or that a translation is wrong.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use quantifier exchange to move the negation. To show that a translation is wrong, describe a small situation in which the English statement and the formula have different truth values. This is the quickest proof.

sections.enonce_markdown: Translate each statement into predicate logic with the letters given. (i) Every yam on this stall is fresh (Yx: $x$ is a yam on this stall; Fx: $x$ is fresh). (ii) No member of the club is a minor (Mx: $x$ is a member of the club; Nx: $x$ is a minor). (iii) Some students are not prefects (Sx: $x$ is a student; Px: $x$ is a prefect). (iv) Only members may vote (Mx: $x$ is a member; Vx: $x$ may vote). (v) Give a second form of (i) without using the universal quantifier. (10 marks)

etapes.justification: Every signals a universal statement, and a universal takes the conditional.
No is universal and negative: for every member, being a minor is excluded.
Some signals the existential quantifier, which takes the conjunction, and not carries the negation on the predicate.
Only reverses the terms: being able to vote requires being a member, not the other way round.

etapes.action: Find a second form of (i) by quantifier exchange.
etapes.justification: A universal statement is false exactly when there is a counter-case, so it can be written as the denial of an existential one.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $\sim(\exists x)(Yx \cdot \sim Fx)$: there is no yam on this stall that is not fresh.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answers: (i) $(x)(Yx \supset Fx)$; (ii) $(x)(Mx \supset \sim Nx)$, or equivalently $\sim(\exists x)(Mx \cdot Nx)$; (iii) $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot \sim Px)$; (iv) $(x)(Vx \supset Mx)$; (v) $\sim(\exists x)(Yx \cdot \sim Fx)$.

items.erreur_markdown: The student writes $(x)(Sx \cdot Px)$ for "All $S$ are $P$".
items.pourquoi_faux: This says that everything in the universe is an S and a P. If there is any non-S, the formula is false even though the English statement may be true.
items.correction_markdown: Use the conditional with the universal quantifier: $(x)(Sx \supset Px)$.

items.erreur_markdown: The student writes $(\exists x)(Sx \supset Px)$ for "Some $S$ are $P$".
items.pourquoi_faux: A conditional is true whenever its antecedent is false, so the formula is true if anything at all is not an S, even when no S is P.
items.correction_markdown: Use the conjunction with the existential quantifier: $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot Px)$.

items.erreur_markdown: The student writes $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot \sim Px)$ for "No $S$ are $P$".
items.pourquoi_faux: That formula is the translation of Some S are not P, which is the contradictory of the universal affirmative, not of the statement given.

items.erreur_markdown: The student writes $(x)(Sx \supset Px)$ for "Only $S$ are $P$".
items.pourquoi_faux: The terms are in the wrong order. This says that every S is a P, whereas the English statement says that every P is an S.

items.erreur_markdown: The student writes $Sx \supset Px$ for "All $S$ are $P$".
items.pourquoi_faux: There is no quantifier, so the formula is an open propositional function and not a proposition.

items.enonce_markdown: Translate with the letters given: (i) Every bus is full (Bx: $x$ is a bus; Fx: $x$ is full). (ii) Some nurses are teachers (Nx: $x$ is a nurse; Tx: $x$ is a teacher). (iii) Kofi is a farmer and Ama is a trader (Fk: Kofi is a farmer; Ta: Ama is a trader).
items.solution_markdown:
(i) **$(x)(Bx \supset Fx)$**, a universal statement with the conditional.
(ii) **$(\exists x)(Nx \cdot Tx)$**, an existential statement with the conjunction.
(iii) **$Fk \cdot Ta$**, a conjunction of two singular statements, with no quantifier.

items.enonce_markdown: Translate with the letters given: (i) None but graduates are eligible (Gx: $x$ is a graduate; Ex: $x$ is eligible). (ii) No pupil is late (Px: $x$ is a pupil; Lx: $x$ is late). (iii) Some roads are not safe (Rx: $x$ is a road; Sx: $x$ is safe). Give a second form of (ii).
items.solution_markdown:
(i) None but is exclusive: eligibility requires being a graduate. **$(x)(Ex \supset Gx)$**.
(ii) **$(x)(Px \supset \sim Lx)$**. A second form is **$\sim(\exists x)(Px \cdot Lx)$**.
(iii) **$(\exists x)(Rx \cdot \sim Sx)$**.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Write "Not all birds fly" (Bx: $x$ is a bird; Fx: $x$ flies) in two equivalent ways. (b) A student writes $(x)(Sx \cdot Px)$ for "All students are present" (Sx: $x$ is a student; Px: $x$ is present). Describe a situation in which the English statement is true and the formula is false. (c) The student writes $(\exists x)(Sx \supset Px)$ for "Some students are present". Describe a situation in which the formula is true and the English statement is false.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The denial of a universal is an existential: **$\sim(x)(Bx \supset Fx)$**, equivalent to **$(\exists x)(Bx \cdot \sim Fx)$**.
(b) Take a room containing two persons: one is a student who is present, the other is not a student. Every student is present, so the English statement is true. But the formula says that every person is a student and is present, which is false because of the second person.
(c) Take the same room, but suppose the only student is absent. The formula is true, because the second person is not a student and so makes the conditional true, while the English statement is false because no student is present. The correct formulas are $(x)(Sx \supset Px)$ and $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot Px)$.

items_markdown: All $S$ are $P$: $(x)(Sx \supset Px)$. No $S$ are $P$: $(x)(Sx \supset \sim Px)$. Some $S$ are $P$: $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot Px)$. Some $S$ are not $P$: $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot \sim Px)$.
Universal quantifier with $\supset$; existential quantifier with $\cdot$.
Quantifier exchange: $\sim(x)Fx \equiv (\exists x)\sim Fx$ and $\sim(\exists x)Fx \equiv (x)\sim Fx$.
Only and none but reverse the terms: $(x)(Px \supset Sx)$; all but needs at least $(x)(\sim Sx \supset Px)$.
A general statement needs a quantifier; check each translation by reading it back in words or by a small counter-situation.
